## Response to Reviewer A3kt

Thank you very much for your constructive feedback. We sincerely appreciate your valuable comments. Regarding the concerns raised, we would like to address them as follows:

**[About the Changes]**

We apologize for not clearly explaining the improvements we plan to make to the paper. In our previous rebuttal (1/2), we conducted all the singing tasks you mentioned (and others not) and provided the experimental results. We will include these in the appendix of the next version of the paper, which aligns with our description of "All Singing Tasks" (or we consider changing it to "All **Current** Singing Tasks").

**[About Realistic Music Scores]**

Thank you for your insightful question. The concepts of realistic music scores (RMS) and fine-grained music scores have been discussed and defined in previous works that utilize music scores for singing tasks. We have cited these references [1,2] in our paper. Additionally, we have distinguished between realistic and fine-grained music scores with illustrations in Figure 3 of our current paper. Furthermore, we have provided a detailed explanation of the advantages of RMS: "Unlike fine-grained music scores, GTSinger uniquely offers realistic music scores featuring regular note duration, assisting singing models in learning and adapting to real-world musical compositions." RMS provides more comprehensive information than previous fine-grained music scores, including alignment, note pitch, note duration, key, type, beats, and more.

Again, we sincerely thank you for your feedback. We will incorporate the contents of this rebuttal into the next version of the paper to reduce any potential misunderstandings.

**[References]**

[1] Zhang, L., Li, R., Wang, S., Deng, L., Liu, J., Ren, Y., He, J., Huang, R., Zhu, J., Chen, X., et al. M4singer: A multi-style, multi-singer and musical score provided mandarin singing corpus. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35:6914–6926, 2022.

## Overall Response

To all reviewers,

We are grateful to each reviewer for the time and effort put into providing valuable suggestions. Your feedback has been instrumental in enhancing our work. We have individually responded to the comments and concerns of each reviewer. Please refer to each response for details.

Regarding the concerns raised by some reviewers about the task applicability of GTSinger, we apologize for not listing and elaborating on "All Singing Tasks" in the paper, which may have caused some confusion. Due to the paper's length limitations, we only provided four benchmarks: "technique-controllable SVS, technique recognition, style transfer, and speech-to-singing (STS) conversion." However, as shown in Figure 1, our dataset, with word-level and phoneme-level lyrics annotation, can be used for automatic lyrics transcription. The manual word-level and phoneme-level alignments we propose also aid in the audio-to-lyrics alignment task. Furthermore, the note pitches and durations provided in the realistic music scores (RMS) make our dataset suitable for singing transcription tasks, while the global labels, such as emotion and singing method labels, support discriminative tasks like emotion recognition and singing method detection. In conclusion, our dataset is applicable to all the singing tasks proposed at this stage. We will also include this information in future versions of our paper.

Additionally, we will continue to refine and update the dataset versions based on user feedback to ensure annotation accuracy and expand variety. As highlighted in Section 5 (Lines 280-288), "our dataset currently lacks diversity in singers and does not include several commonly used singing techniques, such as vocal fry." Future efforts will focus on enhancing the diversity of the singing data. We plan to enrich our dataset by incorporating various singers, singing techniques, languages, and singing methods. Meanwhile, in Section 3, we have detailed the complete process for expanding the GTSinger dataset, including the corresponding data processing pipeline [1], and have referenced existing open-source tools [2,3] that can be used in future work to supplement the dataset according to our pipeline. This process facilitates contributions from others who wish to expand our dataset. 

Once again, we sincerely thank each reviewer for their time and effort in providing valuable suggestions. We hope that our responses have adequately addressed your concerns and we remain open to further discussion.

Best regards,

Authors

## Response to Reviewer A3kt (2/2)

**[About the Usability of the "Fine-grained Music Scores"]**

Thank you for your insightful comments and detailed analyses. However, it seems there is a misunderstanding. In GTSinger, we propose Realistic Music Scores (RMS), which are annotated and adjusted by musical experts, not "Fine-grained Music Scores." As stated in Section 1, "Unlike fine-grained music scores, GTSinger uniquely offers realistic music scores featuring regular note duration, assisting singing models in learning and adapting to real-world musical composition." The RMS provides more comprehensive information than previous fine-grained music scores, including alignment, note pitch, note duration, key, type, beats, and more. Additionally, the comparison between F0, fine-grained music scores, and realistic music scores is shown in Figure 3 of the paper. Real-world composers can directly input realistic music scores for singing voice synthesis, whereas Fine-grained Music Scores require manual annotation, and F0 must be extracted from existing singing, making them less suitable for real-world applications. Moreover, recent state-of-the-art models, such as RMSSinger and StyleSinger, utilize the RMS for singing voice generation, demonstrating its stronger compatibility.

Regarding your concern about the usability of RMS, we not only provide readily usable json files [14] containing note pitch and note duration extracted from musicxml, but we also offer code [15] to process musicxml. As detailed in Section 3.3, we provide all the necessary tools and results to facilitate subsequent related work and expand the dataset.

**[About the Baseline Model]**

We greatly appreciate your comments. In our paper, the selected models are representative state-of-the-art open-source models in the field of singing voice synthesis (SVS), and they achieve good results on our dataset [13]. We choose two traditional top SVS models, DiffSinger and RMSSinger, as well as StyleSinger, a zero-shot SVS model, representing the current best SOTA singing models. No other models surpass these in performance. Future SVS models can be trained on our data to achieve even better results.

Thank you again for your valuable suggestions!

**[References]**

[1] G. Meseguer-Brocal, A. Cohen-Hadria, and G. Peeters, “Dali: A large dataset of synchronized audio, lyrics and notes, automatically created using teacher-student machine learning paradigm,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.10606, 2019.

[2] A. Baevski, Y. Zhou, A. Mohamed, and M. Auli, “wav2vec 2.0: A framework for self-supervised learning of speech representations,” NeurIPS, vol. 33, pp. 12 449–12 460, 2020.

[3] Mirelle, E., Ahlback, S., and Dixon, S. Automatic Lyrics Transcription using Dilated Convolutional Neural Networks with Self-Attention. arXiv preprint arXiv:2007.06486

[4] L. Ou, X. Gu, Y. Wang, "Transfer Learning of wav2vec 2.0 for Automatic Lyric Transcription," arXiv preprint arXiv:2207.09747.

[5] McAuliffe, M., Socolof, M., Mihuc, S., Wagner, M., and Sonderegger, M. Montreal forced aligner: Trainable text-speech alignment using kaldi. In Interspeech, volume 2017, pp. 498–502, 2017.

[6] https://github.com/qiuqiao/SOFA

[7] Li, R., Zhang, Y., Wang, Y., Hong, Z., Huang, R., and Zhao, Z. Robust singing voice transcription serves synthesis, arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.09940.

[8] Yong, S., Su, L., and Nam, J. A phoneme-informed neural network model for notelevel singing transcription. In ICASSP 2023-2023 10 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP), pages 1–5. IEEE.

[9] Chao Li, Xiaokong Ma, Bing Jiang, Xiangang Li, Xuewei Zhang, Xiao Liu, Ying Cao, Ajay Kannan, Zhenyao Zhu. Deep Speaker: an End-to-End Neural Speaker Embedding System. arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.02304.

## Response to Reviewer A3kt (1/2)

Thank you very much for your constructive feedback. We sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestions. Regarding the concerns raised, we would like to address them as follows:

**[About All Singing Tasks]**

We apologize for not listing and elaborating on the "All Singing Tasks" in the paper, which may have caused some confusion. Due to the paper's length limitations, we only provide four benchmarks: "technique-controllable SVS, technique recognition, style transfer, speech-to-singing (STS) conversion." However, as shown in Figure 1, our dataset includes word-level and phoneme-level lyrics annotation, manual phoneme-level alignments, and note information (note pitch and note duration in realistic music scores). This makes our dataset applicable to the common tasks you mentioned as well as other unexplored tasks. Some additional singing-related tasks and their results are as follows:

**Automatic Lyrics Transcription.** Since we provide word-level and phoneme-level lyrics annotation, our dataset can be used for automatic lyrics transcription. We choose one state-of-the-art ASR(automatic speech recognition) model and two state-of-the-art ALT(automatic lyrics Transcription) models. In order to enrich training data's diversity,we use DALI(180h, 5358 audios)[1] and GTSinger together to train the models and choose WER (word error rate) as the evaluation metric. We conduct inference on English songs in GTSinger, and the test results are as follows:

|                 | wav2vec2.0[2] | ALTA[3] | wav2vec2.0(ALT)[4] |
| ---------------- | ------------- | ------- | ------------------ |
| WER $\downarrow$ | 25.40         | 17.63   | 15.85              |

**Audio-to-Lyrics Alignment.** As shown in Figure 1, the manual word-level and phoneme-level alignments we provide also aid in the audio-to-lyrics alignment task. We choose two state-of-the-art audio-to-lyrics alignment models and use GTSinger to align. Two evaluation metrics, word boundaries and phoneme boundaries, are used to evaluate the performance of the models. We conduct inference on English and Chinese songs in GTSinger, and the test results are as follows:

|                       | MFA(en)[5] | SOFA(en)[6] | MFA(zh) | SOFA(zh) |
| ------------------------------ | ---------- | ----------- | ------- | -------- |
| word boundaries (mean) (ms)    | 51.6       | 30.5        | 36.2    | 24.1     |
| phoneme boundaries (mean) (ms) | 32.1       | 23.9        | 20.7    | 17.8     |

**Singing Transcription.** Singing Transcription aims to extract and transcribe information from a singing voice, such as pitch, rhythm, and lyrics. For lyrics, the part on Automatic Lyrics Transcription above demonstrates our usability for this task. For rhythm, as shown in Appendix A.3, "We annotate each group (each song comprising control and technique groups) with global style labels provided by music experts, including pace (slow, moderate, and fast)". Furthermore, you can get rhythm information like BPM (beats per minute), beats, and keys from the RMS (realistic music score) we annotate, all of which can aid in rhythm transcription. For pitch transcription, we propose the note pitch and note duration in json files and RMS. You can easily train pitch transcription models like ROSVOT[7 and MusicYOLO[8] using GTSinger.

**Singer Identification.** As discussed in Section 1, GTSinger comprises 20 singers across nine widely spoken languages. We provide singer information for each audio segment, allowing for the training of singer identification models on the GTSinger dataset. We select three speaker-identification models as baselines and evaluate our identification performance using Accuracy and F1-score as metrics. The results are presented below:

|          | Deep Speaker[9] | SincNet[10] | ATST[11] |
| -------- | --------------- | ----------- | -------- |
| F1       | 0.86            | 0.88        | 0.92     |
| Accuracy | 0.87            | 0.90        | 0.94     |

However, due to the limited number of singers, the singer identification task may still have room for improvement in practical applications. As mentioned in Section 5, we aim to expand the number of singers and languages in GTSinger in the future, thereby increasing the diversity of our dataset and enabling the training of more robust singer identification models.

**Vocal Technique Recognition at the Utterance Level.** As demonstrated in Section 4.2, we successfully implement phoneme-level singing technique recognition and provide phoneme-level singing technique annotations. For the utterance-level technique recognition task, we can integrate all the techniques appearing in a given utterance as the utterance's technique label for training, resulting in an utterance-level Vocal Technique recognizer. We train our singing technique recognizer based on ROSVOT[8], with the test results as follows:

|      | mixed voice | falsetto | breathy | pharyngeal | vibrato | glissando |
| ---- | ----------- | -------- | ------- | ---------- | ------- | --------- |
| F1   | 0.70        | 0.98     | 0.96    | 0.76       | 0.70    | 0.65      |
| Accuracy  | 0.73        | 0.86     | 0.74    | 0.72       | 0.85    | 0.77      |

**Singing Voice Separation.** We greatly appreciate your comments. As GTSinger is a singing corpus that lacks corresponding BGM audio for the vocals, it cannot currently support Singing Voice Separation tasks. However, since Singing Voice Separation is inherently a task within the music domain, we believe this does not detract from our claim that GTSinger is applicable to all singing tasks. Nevertheless, in the future, we will strive to provide accompanying instrumental tracks alongside the clean vocal recordings, thereby contributing to the music domain, including Singing Voice Separation.

In conclusion, our dataset is applicable to all the singing tasks proposed at this stage. We hope our response addresses your concerns. Thank you once again!

## Response to Reviewer kj3W (2/2)

**[Regarding the Quality Assessment of Annotations]**

We appreciate your comments on the annotation quality of our recordings. We acknowledge our reliance on **human expertise** for proposed annotations and alignments. While manual fine-tuning may introduce minor discrepancies, such as alignment offsets of 0.01 seconds, these do not significantly affect tasks related to singing voice synthesis and lyric alignment.

Meanwhile, we have made substantial efforts to ensure the accuracy of annotations. We employ a combination of machine-based coarse annotation and manual fine annotation for alignments and music scores, as detailed in Section 3.3. Additionally, we perform double-checks and post-processing checks for each annotation. We also use automated checks to verify the accuracy of the annotations [1]. These measures aim to minimize human error and maintain high data integrity.

We have also explored the use of various models for assessing annotation quality. However, as noted in Sections 3.3 and 4.2, there remains a considerable discrepancy between model-generated annotations and those made by human experts. Open-source aligners such as MFA [2], SOFA [3], and WhisperX [4], along with tools like technique detectors and emotion classifiers [5], still show a significant gap compared to expert annotations. 

We will continue to refine and update the dataset versions based on user feedback to ensure annotation accuracy. Future work may consider using our carefully annotated data to design and train better models for automatic annotation, enabling more convenient data expansion.

Thank you once again for your constructive feedback.

**[References]**

[1] https://github.com/GTSinger/GTSinger

[2] McAuliffe, M., Socolof, M., Mihuc, S., Wagner, M., and Sonderegger, M. Montreal Forced Aligner: Trainable Text-Speech Alignment Using Kaldi. In Interspeech, volume 2017, pp. 498–502, 2017.

[3] https://github.com/qiuqiao/SOFA

[4] Bain, M., Hun, J., Han, T., Zisserman, A. WhisperX: Time-Accurate Speech Transcription of Long-Form Audio. arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.00747, 2023.

[5] https://hf-mirror.com/speechbrain/emotion-diarization-wavlm-large

## Response to Reviewer kj3W (1/2)

We would like to express our deepest gratitude for your positive feedback and insightful comments. Below, we have addressed your concerns in detail.

**[Regarding the Quality Assessment of Recordings]**

We sincerely appreciate your feedback on the quality assessment of our recordings. Your suggestions are invaluable and align closely with our ongoing efforts to enhance the quality of our dataset. Our **pruning strategy** for singing data currently involves music experts who evaluate various metrics, including singing quality and technical contrast. Initially, we conduct a basic quality assessment based on the audio's sampling rate, bandwidth, and bit depth, and have made the code available to facilitate further expansion of the dataset by others [1]. However, subjective standards such as technical contrast and expressiveness are challenging to assess using existing methods. To improve the accuracy of our data pruning, we have engaged multiple music experts in discussions and voting to ensure the high quality of the GTSinger corpus. Looking forward, future work may involve designing and training models using our carefully curated data to assess the quality of singing voice data automatically, thereby streamlining the data pruning process.

## Response to Reviewer pxTo (2/2) 

**[Regarding Impact and Application]**

We greatly appreciate the reviewer's suggestion to summarize the potential impact and applications of the proposed dataset. We provide a detailed explanation here, which we will include in the final version of the paper.

First, concerning the **available tasks** for our dataset: As mentioned in the paper, the dataset we propose can be used for a wide range of singing-related tasks. Section 4 outlines four downstream tasks based on our dataset, covering the major singing voice generation tasks. Additionally, as shown in Figure 1, our dataset, with word-level and phoneme-level lyrics annotation, can be used for automatic lyrics transcription. The manual word-level and phoneme-level alignments we propose also aid in the audio-to-lyrics alignment task. Furthermore, the note pitches and durations provided in the realistic music scores (RMS) make our dataset suitable for singing transcription tasks, while the global labels, such as emotion and singing method labels, support discriminative tasks like emotion recognition and singing method detection.

Regarding **real-world applications and potential impact**: As stated in Section 1 (Lines 26-28), the scarcity of publicly available, high-quality, multi-task singing datasets has become a significant bottleneck in the development of singing-related tasks. Our GTSinger aims to advance the field. Moreover, the singing voice synthesis (SVS) task via RMS can assist music creators and composers in directly generating singing voices or songs through SVS systems, thereby significantly supporting their creative process.
Additionally, models trained on our dataset enable more controllable and personalized applications. These include providing voiceovers for short entertainment videos, allowing people who are not skilled in singing to customize their own professional and melodious singing voices, aiding singers in creating more works, supporting virtual singers, and offering valuable tools in professional composition.

**[References]**

[1] https://github.com/GTSinger/GTSinger

[2] McAuliffe, M., Socolof, M., Mihuc, S., Wagner, M., and Sonderegger, M. Montreal Forced Aligner: Trainable Text-Speech Alignment Using Kaldi. In Interspeech, volume 2017, pp. 498–502, 2017.

[3] Li, R., Zhang, Y., Wang, Y., Hong, Z., Huang, R., and Zhao, Z. Robust Singing Voice Transcription Serves Synthesis. arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.09940, 2024.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces GTSinger, a new singing voice dataset comprising 80 hours of singing voice from 20 different singers across nine languages. The dataset is enriched with multiple annotations, including phoneme-level singing techniques, phoneme-to-audio alignments, global style labels, and music scores. Additionally, paired speech audio is provided. The authors detail the dataset and demonstrate its usability through benchmark experiments in technique-controlled singing voice synthesis, singing technique recognition, singing voice style transfer, and speech-to-singing conversion.

review.value:
The paper is clearly written and easy to follow, making it accessible to a broad audience. The detailed description of the dataset creation process is commendable, providing transparency and clarity. One of the significant strengths of this paper is the large-scale data with multiple annotations, including phoneme-level singing techniques, phoneme-to-audio alignments, global style labels, and music scores.
The authors have referenced adequate and relevant papers, situating their work within the broader context of singing voice synthesis research. The benchmark experiments and evaluations conducted are sound, demonstrating the dataset's utility and robustness. The inclusion of cross-lingual evaluation adds depth to the analysis, highlighting the dataset's versatility.

The appendix is valuable, offering a detailed data creation process that can guide future researchers in scaling up data collection efforts. Additionally, the statistical analysis in the appendix provides a comprehensive overview of the data, enhancing the paper's thoroughness.

The choice of a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license for the dataset supports reproducible research, encouraging further innovation in the field. Given the dataset's scope and the evaluation, GTSinger will have a significant impact on singing voice synthesis and adjacent fields of research.

title.value: This is a well written paper, directly relevant to the NeurIPS datasets & benchmarks track, which has created a fairly large-scale (for its domain) dataset on multi-lingual singing and associated metadata, evaluated across a range of mostly generative taks.

summary_and_contributions.value:
* Large scale (for its domain) open dataset of singing recordings and rich associated metadata.
* Effort to create a multilingual dataset, ensuring dataset diversity.
* Evaluation on four donwstream tasks.

review.value:
This is a well written and well organized Datasets & Benchmarks paper on creating a fairly large scale (for the application domain) paper on singing audio and associated metadata on a multilingual level, spanning also several vocal techniques and good rich metadata. This is evaluated on a series of four downstream tasks, three out of which are on the generative side and one on the discriminative side. 

Overall this is a very good paper and dataset contribution. The data collection process was carried out in an open and transparent way, and singer consent has been obtained as to make the data open and available. The metadata collected along with the recordings is rich and there are several possible downstream tasks where the proposed dataset can be applied to - noting though that the list of tasks currently evaluated veers more on the generative side, therefore missing some common and useful discriminative tasks where the proposed dataset could probe useful (and therefore making the claim in the title "All Singing Tasks" a bit of a stretch, and in my opinion should be removed - more information can be found in the below review). Still, this is overall impressive work and it's a well designed contribution which I recommend for publication. 

Specific comments:

* As mentioned above, the paper mentions "All Singing Tasks", which could be termed misleading. In the sense that although the dataset could eventually prove useful for several tasks related to singing, the current evaluations are only made on four downstream tasks, 3 of them being generative and one being discriminative. There are however many other downstream tasks related to singing which are not mentioned at all in the manuscript, and also relevant datasets for those tasks are also not discussed at all. These include: singing voice separation (i.e. separating singing voice from accompaniment), automatic lyrics transcription (i.e. the equivalent task to automatic speech recognition but for singing - plus related tasks such as phoneme transcription), audio-to-lyrics alignment (i.e. automatically aligning audio recordings containing singing to lyrics text), and finally singing transcription (i.e. pitch or note level transcription of singing voice). There are other under-explored tasks too, such as singer identification or vocal technique recognition at an utterance level (as opposed to a clip level as was done here). Given all the above, I would recommend that the scope of this work, the related discussion on limitations, the title, the description of related work, are all revised as to reflect the above.

*  Section 3.3: I have some concerns on the usability of the "finegrained music scores" in musicXML format. Common practice for singing transcription would either focus on a reference score (which can be interpreted in various ways by a singer) or would focus on an F0 curve or pitch transcription as shown in Fig. 3(a). It would be difficult for a human to interpret this finegrained score, and it is difficult to understand which donwstream tasks can benefit from this representation.

* Section 4 could benefit from including additional baseline systems for each downstream task considered. The authors have done good work on including appropriate models for each task, but it is not clear how performance would compare with other state of the art models for the same task.

strengths.value:
* High quality, and large scale (for its domain) open dataset of singing recordings and rich associated metadata.
* Clear effort by the authors to create a multilingual dataset, ensuring dataset and cultural diversity which is often absent from similar research domains.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
As mentioned in the review above: 
* Consider wider range of tasks available for singing voice analysis and generation, and cite relevant work and relevant datasets for the tasks mentioned in the review field above.
* Consider the usability of the "finegrained music scores" in musicXML format and delete if not relevant for specific downstream tasks.
* Consider including additional baseline systems for each task for comparison.

limitations.value: The authors do attempt to consider limitations of the proposed work, although perhaps this section can be expanded through the comments made above.

correctness.value: Overall the choice of methods for constructing and evaluating the dataset is completely sound, and I do not have any concerns on the technical correctness of this work.

clarity.value: The paper is generally very well written, clear, and well structured. No comments on presentation.

relation_to_prior_work.value: As mentioned in the review above, the paper does not include nor cite works and datasets which are on computational analysis of singing voice related to various tasks, including but not limited to: singing voice separation, automatic lyrics transcription, audio-to-lyrics alignment, and singing transcription - plus other emerging tasks mentioned in the review field above. Given the claims made in the paper, it would be appropriate to consider wider computational research carried out on singing voice beyond the tasks considered in the paper.

documentation.value: There is good amount of detail and documentation regarding dataset collection, statistics, and dataset availability. Ethical and responsible use are also covered well in supplementary material. No comments or concerns here.

ethics.value: This work was overall designed in a responsible way with respect to obtaining singer consent for recording and annotation, and care has also been taken to prevent subject identity. No major ethical issues were identified.

title.value: GTSinger: A Global Multi-Technique Singing Corpus with Realistic Music Scores for All Singing Tasks

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors introduce GTSinger, a comprehensive and high-quality dataset featuring meticulously annotated multi-technique singing recordings freely accessible to the research community. They emphasize the inclusion of realistic music scores to facilitate real-world composition and the availability of paired data for speech-to-singing tasks. Additionally, the authors conduct benchmark experiments using state-of-the-art techniques, presenting a well-defined evaluation strategy that underscores the dataset's utility and versatility.

review.value: The paper is well-written, making it a pleasure to read and easy to follow. It is generally very well structured and includes experiments relevant to real-world composition applications. The state-of-the-art section is well-organized, clearly highlighting the strengths of the presented dataset. The figures are highly detailed, effectively illustrating the data acquisition process. The data description is thorough, supporting its use in future research. The evaluation strategy for each presented task is well-structured and summarized in tables. This paper provides a detailed description of a high-quality dataset suitable for music composition, accompanied by well-organized benchmark experiments to facilitate further research.

strengths.value:
- The paper is well-structured and supported by comprehensive tables and figures clearly illustrating the contributions.
- The data acquisition process and the proposed pipeline are thoroughly described, offering a clear strategy for expanding the dataset.
- The annotations and features in the dataset are well-documented and supported by histograms that provide insightful visual representations.
- The comparison with other available datasets demonstrates the superior potential of GTSinger for training models in multi-singing tasks and speech-to-singing applications.
- The benchmark experiments underscore the dataset's applicability for real-world composition tasks.
- The evaluation strategy and metrics employed establish a robust baseline for future research in the field.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The dataset presented in this paper stands out for its exceptional quality, particularly regarding the meticulous annotation and data post-processing strategies employed. However, annotations also seem to depend heavily on human annotators' expertise. To further improve these aspects, the authors could consider incorporating methods for data pruning and quality assessment of recordings and annotations, focusing on managing annotation uncertainty. Including such methods would establish a robust baseline for future research and support the consistent extension of the dataset from other sources.

limitations.value: Yes, Limitations and Social Impact is well written in the outlook

clarity.value: The paper is well-structured and supported by comprehensive tables and figures clearly illustrating the contributions.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
- The comparison with other available datasets is provided
- Benchmark experiments provide an overview of some state-of-the-art approaches

documentation.value: The paper is supplemented with extensive additional material and appendices, accessible through corresponding links. Notably, the authors have made both the code and the dataset available, facilitating transparency and enabling other researchers to replicate and build upon their work.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
